doc.title: Orrin Keepnews interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 7, 2002

chapter: Monk, the Army and learning the job
title: Miles Davis's remarks and the 1954 Miles-Monk session
summary: He discounts Miles's complaint about Monk, praises Miles and the sextet, and notes both men's baiting.

story.theme_name: Playing with and around Miles Davis
story.community_name: Playing with Miles Davis: joining, sessions and the band

blocks.x: I had come across this comment from Miles Davis—
Well comments from Miles Davis should be taken with grains of salt. But what did Miles say?

He was listening to Sonny Rollins with Thelonious Monk, “The Way You Look Tonight,” and he says, “I don’t see how a record company can record something like that. You know the way Monk plays he never gives any support to a rhythm section. When I had him on my date I had him lay out.” You know, has there been circumstances—

Oh come on he had him lay out on one tune, the whole celebrated story, as Monk has said, there never was any danger of there being a fight because I would have killed him. And he’s right. Despite all the photos of Miles in boxing gear. Miles, this is a whole other subject but you brought Miles into it. Miles Davis, who I never worked with but who I knew pretty well over a very long period of time, and basically I’m going to say just in the whole pantheon of things, not that he ever asked me to but I approve of Miles Davis as a player. I think that Miles was an incredibly important player. I think that the Miles Davis, THE Miles Davis Sextet, which among other things had a couple of artists in it who I have worked with very closely over the years, was perhaps the seminal group in quote modern jazz. I mean that sextet and with either of the drummers in it, whether it was Philly Joe, who was only briefly in the sextet, or Jimmy Cobb, who is now its only surviving member, but that was a wonderful group. Miles was, in terms of ideas, in terms of execution, I’m among those who like Miles as a trumpet player. You can get into arguments about that. But Miles as a maker of deliberately controversial statements is another whole thing. If you take seriously, on the surface, what Miles says under certain circumstances, as somebody did because what you just quoted got picked up and published and immortalized, if you took it seriously you were playing Miles’ game. That’s all. Miles was an agent provocateur of the first order. And so that, and you have to also understand that he was not the only one like that. There’s a lot, there’s a lot of this people-baiting that goes on in Monk too. And Monk would — well Monk was supposed to be very difficult to understand, just conversationally I mean, not musically. And that was one of the things that was always very strange to me because the first time I met him we sat down and I did an interview with him and I had no problem whatsoever. I subsequently discovered it was very simple. He was as easy or difficult to understand as he wanted to be. I think you could probably — I claimed you could chart it and come out with about seven different levels of intelligibility, as he wanted to play the game under particular circumstances. So above all Miles and Monk coming into association with each other are coming in conflict as in the date that Miles is talking about, that famous Christmas eve 1954 session with Milt Jackson and etcetera. That must have been a hell of a date to be a fly on the wall at because these two personalities, each of whom always

demanded to be the centerpiece, to be the focal point of what was going on, to be in control, coming head to head, actually it is a wonder that they didn’t really start duking it out together. But Monk said they didn’t because he would have killed him. But anyway you must — particularly when you’re dealing with famous remarks and famous incidents, try to look behind the surface as much as you can.
Okay. With a whole bag of salt.
